title: One Helix Decides On or Off

scenes.tts: Inject a rat with radioactive estradiol, and almost every tissue lets the hormone go again. The uterus and the vagina keep it. Estradiol is a steroid, and a steroid dissolves in fat. So it crosses the cell membrane on its own, and nothing on the outer surface has to receive it. What inside the cell is built to catch it?
scenes.visual: Two cells side by side. Estradiol enters both; in 'most tissues' it leaves again, in 'uterus and vagina' it stays. One big cell: the hormone passes through the membrane, a crossed-out surface receptor sits outside, and a dashed question-mark box inside holds the hormone.
scenes.narration: Inject a rat with radioactive estradiol, and almost every tissue lets the hormone go again. The uterus and the vagina keep it. Estradiol is a steroid, and a steroid dissolves in fat. So it crosses the cell membrane on its own, and nothing on the outer surface has to receive it. What inside the cell is built to catch it?

scenes.tts: The protein that catches the hormone is a receptor, and it is one chain with two grips. One region closes around the hormone, and another takes hold of a specific short stretch of D N A. No second messenger is made, and no kinase cascade runs. A transcription factor is a protein that binds D N A and controls whether a gene is copied into R N A. The receptor is one.
scenes.caption: The protein that catches the hormone is a receptor, and it is one chain with two grips. One region closes around the hormone, and another takes hold of a specific short stretch of DNA. No second messenger is made, and no kinase cascade runs. A transcription factor is a protein that binds DNA and controls whether a gene is copied into RNA. The receptor is one.
scenes.visual: The question-mark box becomes the receptor: a hormone-binding block with a pocket, a hinge, and a DNA-binding block. The hormone drops into the pocket, DNA rises and the lower block grips a short stretch of it. Second messenger and kinase cascade boxes are crossed out; an arrow runs from the receptor to the gene.

scenes.tts: The moving part is helix 12, the last helix of the hormone-binding domain. An agonist is a molecule that switches the receptor on. With one in the pocket, helix 12 folds across the mouth like a lid, and that completes a shallow groove. A helper protein called a co-activator carries a short helix, L X X L L, that fits the groove. The groove is the hormone's whole message.

scenes.visual: The hormone-binding domain fills the frame. Helix 12 stands up beside the pocket holding estradiol, then swings down across the mouth like a lid; a dashed groove on the surface turns solid. A co-activator drops its short helix into the groove.

scenes.tts: DNA in the nucleus is wound around proteins called histones. Tightly packed DNA is hard to copy into R N A. A co-activator brings enzymes that add acetyl groups to histones. That loosens the packing and helps R N A polymerase start. Then the gene can switch on.
scenes.caption: DNA in the nucleus is wound around proteins called histones. Tightly packed DNA is hard to copy into RNA. A co-activator brings enzymes that add acetyl groups to histones. That loosens the packing and helps RNA polymerase start. Then the gene can switch on.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to the receptor on DNA, co-activator still in the groove. Three histone discs sit packed on the DNA. The co-activator's enzymes drop acetyl badges onto the discs, the discs spread apart, RNA polymerase lands on the gene and the gene turns green.

scenes.tts: An antagonist is a molecule that occupies the receptor without switching it on. The liver converts tamoxifen into forms that bind the receptor much more tightly, such as four hydroxy tamoxifen. That molecule fits the pocket, but one side chain is too long to stay inside. It sticks out where the lid should close. Instead, helix 12 lies in the groove itself, so the co-activator has nowhere to bind.
scenes.visual: Back at the domain: the co-activator lifts away, the lid opens and estradiol leaves. A red tamoxifen dot appears above the pocket, is named 4-hydroxytamoxifen and drops in, with a side chain sticking out of the mouth. The lid starts to close, is blocked, then lies down inside the groove. The co-activator comes back, finds the groove taken and is turned away.

scenes.tts: Tamoxifen blocks the action of estrogen in the breast, yet it imitates estrogen in bone and in the uterus. The receptor with tamoxifen in its pocket still binds D N A. What happens next could depend on the helper proteins each tissue makes. Keep this rule: where helix 12 lies decides whether the groove is free for a co-activator.

scenes.visual: The tamoxifen receptor shrinks into three columns: breast (blocks estrogen), bone and uterus (imitate estrogen), each on DNA with different helper proteins beside it. Then two receptors side by side: lid closed with the groove free, and helix 12 in the groove with the groove taken.
